newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: London robustas tipped to open US$30-$60 higher.
newsitem.headline: London robustas tipped to open US$30-$60 higher.

text.p: London robusta futures are pegged to open US$30-$60 higher later on Wednesday mainly on the back of followthrough buying after a sharp overnight rally in New York arabicas, regional coffee traders said.
"London has a better rally potential than New York," one trader said. "It should be $40-$60 higher this afternoon."
"It's the silly season. I don't know if London's rise is just emotional, but it should up at least $30," another dealer said.

The benchmark September LIFFE robusta futures contract rallied for a hefty $132 gain to close on Tuesday at $1,910 a tonne on commission house buying, a rebound in New York and bullish U.S. consumer stocks data.
September arabicas in New York rose 9.10 cents on the day to end on Tuesday at 190.70 U.S. cents a lb.

The Green Coffee Association of New York reported on Tuesday that U.S. coffee warehouse stocks rose in May by 122,000 60-kg bags, to 1,977,000 bags. Most industry participants expected a build of 150,000-250,000 bags.
"I think $1,980 to $2,000 will be the resistance in London," a dealer said.
One Asian trader said the London market posted larger gains mainly due to the belief that robusta prices still have to catch up to the high levels arabica futures have set in New York.
"More and more people are riding on the sentiment that robustas are undervalued," a dealer said.
Another dealer said that on the numbers, London should be up $40 but that the market has been gyrating so widly across the board it was difficult to predict how it will really perform.
"This market has been so unpredictable that the due up can easily be wrong," he said.
The sharp swings in prices prompted Indonesian coffee farmers and exporters to stay glued to the sidelines.
"It's a bit difficult to find coffee beans in Indonesia at the moment. I think they're waiting for prices to move up again. The Indonesians are holding off a bit," one dealer said.
The Indonesians were badly disapointed when prices nose-dived recently to just under $1,400 a tonne FOB Lampung from a peak about three weeks ago of $2,300 a tonne on the same basis.
The price of Indonesia's benchmark Grade 4, 80 defects, was seen by the trade at around $1,630-$1,680 a tonne FOB Lampung against last week's quote of $1,535-$1,585.
"People in Indonesia were a bit disappointed prices could fluctuate so much. They're a bit wary now," another trader said.

Traders still expect Indonesia's coffee output to be down between 20-30 percent in the current 1996/97 (July-June) season and ignored a recent U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) forecast the crop will reach 456,000 tonnes this year.
Last week, the chairman of the Association of Indonesian Coffee Exporters, Oesman Soedargo, told Reuters he expected 1997 production to plunge by 160,000 tonnes to 290,000 tonnes from 1996.
Vietnamese coffee trade is moribund, waiting for the next harvest towards the end of November, traders said.
"Vietnam is finished," a dealer said. "Business is basically slow."

The price of Vietnam's key Grade 2 coffee, 8.0 percent black and broken, was indicated at around $1,590-$1,610 a tonne FOB Saigon, but very few supplies remained and there were no firm bids in the market, dealers said.
Trading in the Singapore Commodity Exchange (SICOM) reached a paltry 40 lots on Tuesday.

Some 20 lots of the January contract were settled at $1,641 a tonne, 10 lots of the November contract finished at $1,646 a tonne and 10 lots of the September contract ended at $1,649 a tonne, SICOM said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65-8703305)
